lawyer:
Md. Fazlul Karim with Kazi Anowar Hossain, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner.
AY Masihuzzaman, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Captain Shamsul Alam Chowdhury ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Shirin Alam Chowdhury ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
On 28.9.87 the petitioner filed the suit No. 10 of 1987 in Family Court for decree for restitution of conjugal rights against the opposite party. The opposite party also filed, a Family Court Suit No. 5 of 1987 in the same Court prior to the aforesaid suit filed by the petitioner wherein she prayed for a declaration that the matrimonial relation between her and the petitioner did not exist and there was matrimonial separation between them. 

 3. The case of the petitioner as stated in his plaint in the aforesaid suit No. 10 of 1987 in short is that he obtained Master Mariner (Certificate of Competency) from the Ministry of Transport, Government of United Kingdom and served with various foreign Shipping Companies and in 1968 he joined National Shipping Corporation of Pakistan as a Captain and thereafter joined Bangladesh Shipping Corporation and served in that post till April, 1977. Thereafter the petitioner left Bangladesh to join Shipping Companies abroad and in April, 1981 he joined the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Corporation and became its Chairman in 1984 and retired therefrom in May, 1988. The petitioner married the opposite party on 5.9.70 and he had a daughter born to the opposite party on 25.7.71 and the second daughter was born to them on 27.7.79. The petitioner had taken care of and given attention to the opposite party and tried to live a happy conjugal life and the petitioner took the opposite party to the different parts of the world while he was serving abroad. While living together at Dhaka the petitioner helped the opposite party to build up the first floor of her father's house at 69 Gulshan Avenue. The petitioner had a bank account with Barclays Bank Finance Company (Jersey) Ltd., at Channel Island, and out of love and affection for the opposite party and security for her life allowed the opposite party to become a joint holder of the said account of the Bank in which there was substantial amount. The petitioner had given the opposite party's elder brother Mohammad Ali Quayyum who resided at London a power of attorney for the operation of the said bank account. The petitioner for further security of the opposite party's life was appointed as a nominee of the petitioner in an insurance policy of Taka 60,000.00 and to help and aid their aforesaid children he purchased Bonus Savings Certificates for Taka 10,000.00. The petitioner stated in his plaint that in spite of all the endeavors made by him to give all the facilities and comfort to opposite party's life and that of their children, the relation between him and the opposite party began to deteriorate from June, 1984 and thereafter when the petitioner began to reside at his official residence in November, 1984 he persuaded the opposite party along with their children to live with him, but of no avail and subsequently the petitioner came to know that the opposite party had filed the Family Court suit No. 5 of 1987 for dissolution of marriage. The opposite party had filed the said suit, inter alia, on the ground that the petitioner led a life beneath standard to which sit‘ and their children were accustomed to and that the petitioner did not take proper medical advice for treatment of his illness. She further contended that he used to come back late at night and on query he hurled abuses at her and also assaulted her physically. Further she stated that the petitioner did not take any care for the well-being of their children nor he made any attempt to persuade her to live with him and thereby the petitioner miserably failed to discharge his marital obligations. 

 5. On 28.3.90 the learned Assistant Judge allowed only three letters written by the father of the opposite party to the petitioner to be marked Exhibits and the prayer of the petitioner in respect of other documents were rejected. Being aggrieved by the order, the petitioner preferred an appeal before the District Judge Dhaka being Family Misc. Appeal No. 71 of 1990 under section 17 of the Family Courts Ordinance 1985 and on 18.4.90 the memorandum of the aforesaid appeal was rejected on the ground that the same was not maintainable in law. 

 7. A counter affidavit on behalf of the opposite party has been filed controverting the material facts in the petition stating, inter alia, that the opposite party had instituted TS(F) No. 5 of 1987 on 6.6.87 for dissolution of marriage and the petitioner filed the written statement on 14.11.87 and then filed TS(F) No. 10 of 1987 for restitution of conjugal right on 24.11.87 which showed that the petitioner from the very inception was trying to delay the proceeding under one plea or the other just to harass the opposite party. The opposite party has submitted that there is no provision in the Family Courts Ordinance for any appeal or revision against any interlocutory order. Section 17 of the Family Courts Ordinance provides for only one appeal against the judgment, decree and order of the Family Court before the District Judge. The opposite party has also filed a supplementary affidavit stating that the present revisional application was not  maintainable on the ground that there are two family court cases that is TS(F) No. 5 of 1987 and TS(F) No. 10 of 1987 pending in the Second Court of the Assistant Judge, Dhaka which were being heard analogously and so against any order of the said two suits there ought to have been two appeals, and against the order of the said appeals there should have been two revisional application before this Court. 

 8. Mr. Md. Fazlul Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, has, inter alia's submitted that the Assistant Judge committed an error of law in refusing to allow the documents produced in the Court by the petitioner as exhibits and in the facts and circumstances this decision has caused a failure of justice in the case. He has also submitted that the appellate Court has refused to exercise his own jurisdiction on a misconception that there was no appeal against an order passed by the Family Court. 

 9. Mr. AY Masihuzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, has submitted that section 17 of the Family Courts Ordinance does not provide for an appeal against an interlocutory order. The order mentioned in section 17 must be read as a final order of the court. In this connection he has referred to section 24 of the Family Courts Ordinance where he submits that word 'order' referred to in section 17 of the Ordinance means the final order of the court. En order to consider the above submission made by the respective lawyers, we need to look into the provision of the Family Courts Ordinance. 

 10. Section 17 of the Family Courts Ordinance reads as follows : 

 "(1) Subject to the provisions of sub-section (2), an appeal shall lie from a judgment, decree or order of a Family Court to the Court of District Judge. 

 (2) No appeal shall lie from a decree passed by a Family Court. 

 Provided that the Court of District Judge, May, for sufficient cause, extend the said period. 

 (5) A certified copy of the judgment, decree or order of the Court from which the appeal is preferred shall be attached with the appeal. 

 (6) Any order passed by the Court of District Judge shall as soon as may be, be communicated to the Family Court which shall modify or amend the judgment, decree or order accordingly and shall also make necessary entries to that effect in the appropriate column in the register of decrees." 

 11. The word 'order' has not been defined in the Ordinance, and that being so the lawyer appearing for the petitioner has submitted that the word 'order' in section 17 should be interpreted in the ordinary sense of the word and therefore should include all orders passed by the Family Court including interlocutory order. Mr. Masihuzzaman, on the other hand, submits that the Family Courts Ordinance was promulgated with the purpose of speedy disposal of matrimonial cases and therefore the word order appearing in section 17 should be read to mean the final order of the court. As already mentioned above Mr. Masihuzzaman has referred to section 24 of the Family Courts Ordinance, which reads as follows : 

 "(1) A Family Court shall be deemed to be a District Court for the purposes of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (VIII of 1890), and notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, shall, in dealing with matters specified in that Act, follow the procedure specified in that Act, 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (VIII of 1890), an appeal from an order made by a Family Court as District Court under that Act shall lie to the Court of District Judge, and the provisions of section 17 shall apply to such appeal." 

 He has argued that this section provides for appeal from an order made by the Family Court under Guardians and Wards Act 1890 shall lie to the Court of the District Judge and the provision of section 17 shall apply to such appeal. In this section there is no mention of judgment or decree but only "an order". He therefore submits that the word order used in section 17 of the Family Court Ordinance means no other order other than the final order. This may well have been the intention of the legislators that the word order has not been defined in the Ordinance, I would hesitate to read such meaning as being intended by the legislators. The reference to the words 'an order' in section 24 of the Ordinance by itself does not conclusively or satisfactorily show that the word order used in section 17 means final order. In the absence of definition of the word order we have to give the ordinary meaning of the word which means the formal expression of any decision by Court. 

 12. In the case of Moinuddin Md. Vs. Amina Khan Mojlish reported in 42 DLR (1990) page 483 referred to by the lawyer for the petitioner, to plaintiff respondent instituted Money Suit No. 15 of 1986 before the Family Court (3rd Court of Munsif) Dhaka against the defendant appellant for recovery of Dower Money and maintenance under the provisions of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985. On receipt of the summons the defendant appeared and filed a written statement and the suit was fixed for pretrial hearing on 4.3.87. The defendant-appellant filed an application for amendment of the written statement under Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the Family Court by its order dated 1.4.87 rejected the application for amendment of the pleadings on the ground that the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure had no application to the proceedings before the Family Court. Against the aforesaid order dated 1.4.87 passed by the Family Court the defendant appellant filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 118 of 1987 before the Court of the District Judge, Dhaka under section 17(1) of the Family Courts Ordinance. The Miscellaneous Appeal was admitted by the learned District Judge and it was fixed for hearing on 4-6-88 on which date a petition for adjournment of hearing of the Miscellaneous Appeal was filed by the defendant-appellant but the petition for adjournment was rejected and the appeal dismissed for default. Thereafter on 2-7-88 the appellant filed an application under Order 41 rule 19 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure being Miscellaneous Case No. 135 of 1988, for remission of the appeal dismissed for default, and the learned District Judge by the impugned judgment and order dated 9.7.88 rejected the application as not maintainable on the ground that the Court of District Judge being a Family Court under the Family Courts Ordinance, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure (except sections 10 and 11) including the provisions of Order 41 rule 19 were not applicable. Against the said order a Civil Revision was filed before the Division Bench of this Court in which the rule was made absolute. 

 13. Although the question whether there would be an appeal from an order passed by the Family Court would lie before the District Judge was not considered in the said Civil Revision but the rule was made absolute against an order passed by the District Judge on an appeal made to it under section 17(1) of the Family Courts Ordinance. 

 15. With regard to the point that there being two suits before the Family Court there ought to have been two appeals before the District Judge and two revisions before this Court I do not agree with the submission. If the family court had either decreed or dismissed any of the suits then that would give rise to two appeals against the decree or dismissal before the District Judge and thereby necessitating two revisions before this Court. In the instant case two suits were being heard analogously and an order was passed in respect of documents relating to both the suits being heard analogously. Therefore one appeal against such order was in accordance with law and did not require two appeals and two revisional applications. Therefore the submission made by the learned lawyer for the opposite party is not tenable. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the learned District Judge is directed to hear and dispose of the appeal made by the petitioner under section 17 of the Family Courts Ordinance on merit in accordance with law. There will be no order as to costs.
